lead.headline: Enverus says about 90% of AI's water footprint is consumed at the power plant, not the data center
lead.dek: A new Enverus study puts $25 a month of frontier AI use at about 1.9 gallons of water, power generation included, and shifts the siting debate toward the grid.
body: Enverus Intelligence Research published a study on November 24 that measures the water footprint of AI inference against the same monthly spending level. Its base case puts $25 a month of frontier large language model use at about 1.9 gallons of water consumed, including the water used to generate the electricity. The same $25 spent on household electricity from an all gas grid comes to 31 gallons, on almond milk 308 gallons, and on public golf course green fees 679 gallons.

The central finding is where the water goes. Enverus estimates that about 90% of the water attributed to AI inference is consumed at the power plant rather than at the data center itself, a point that matters more as developers turn to natural gas generation for new campuses. On a land basis, it puts a modern hyperscale campus at about 32,100 gallons per acre per month, below irrigated rice, almonds and alfalfa and roughly in line with an average US golf course.

Ryan Luther, director of energy transition research at Enverus, said water use is a real factor in siting but that "the numbers people quote rarely have a consistent basis." The comparison is normalized by spending, so it says little about a single campus drawing on a stressed local aquifer or river. It does suggest that the bigger water decision is often the choice of power supply and cooling at the generating plant.

pipe.source: Most of the water tied to AI is drawn by power plants, so the grid's water source matters as much as the campus's.
pipe.treat: Cooling water at gas and thermal plants is treated and cycled; that is where most AI related consumption happens.
pipe.use: Enverus puts $25 a month of frontier AI use at about 1.9 gallons consumed, power generation included.
pipe.reuse: The study does not size reuse; reclaimed water for plant and campus cooling is one lever operators can weigh.
pipe.discharge: Water that evaporates in plant and campus cooling towers is consumed and does not return to the basin.

use.text: Power sourcing and plant cooling now belong in the water section of a siting study.
Expect questions on water per megawatt hour, not only gallons per server hall.
Dry cooled or reuse supplied generation may become a selling point for AI campuses.
Rules aimed only at data center cooling miss most of the water AI consumes.

briefs.headline: Illinois regulators grant American Water's Illinois unit $74 million, 41% less than it asked
briefs.text: The Illinois Commerce Commission on November 24 approved a $74 million rate increase for Illinois American Water, cutting $53 million from the $127 million the utility requested in January. The commission set return on equity at 9.67%, below the 10.75% requested and the current 9.84%, and widened the low income discount to households earning up to 300% of the federal poverty level. The utility serves about 1.3 million people in 148 communities and has not yet calculated the bill impact.
briefs.why: A sub 10% equity return in a large American Water state is a data point for every pending water rate case and for the Essential merger math.

briefs.headline: Fiji declares a nationwide state of disaster as El Niño drought reaches crisis level
briefs.text: Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka declared a nationwide state of disaster on November 18 after Cabinet accepted advice from the National Disaster Risk Management Council that the drought response had reached crisis thresholds. The declaration lasts up to 30 days at a time and can be extended. Rabuka said remote and maritime communities face growing pressure on their water supplies, and the Fiji Meteorological Service expects below normal rainfall through early 2027 as El Niño strengthens.
briefs.why: Small island supply runs on rain and thin aquifers. A strong El Niño tests emergency desalination, water carting and tank storage across the Pacific.

briefs.headline: Final EPA PFAS test round lifts the count of Americans with PFAS in tap water to about 197 million
briefs.text: The Environmental Working Group said on November 19 that the last installment of EPA's UCMR 5 monitoring, which covered 29 PFAS, plus recent state tests, put about 197 million people on water with detectable PFAS. UCMR 5 found 3,595 sites with detections, bringing the known total to 13,459. EWG, an advocacy group, said EPA is in the final stages of dropping limits for GenX, PFBS, PFNA and PFHxS while keeping 4 parts per trillion limits for PFOA and PFOS, with compliance pushed to 2031.
briefs.why: The national data set is now complete. Utilities that detect PFOA or PFOS have a clearer target and more time, while treatment suppliers have a firmer pipeline.

briefs.headline: Lake Powell rises more than 20 feet after record fall rain, but basin talks remain stalled
briefs.text: Record fall rain in the Four Corners lifted Lake Powell more than 20 feet, and Reclamation forecasts the reservoir staying above 3,500 feet, the level that matters for hydropower and Glen Canyon Dam releases, over the next year. Snowpack is at 70% of median and forecast uncertainty grows after April 30. Utah commissioner Gene Shawcroft noted the lake is still four feet below a year ago, and the seven basin states have not agreed on post 2026 operating rules.
briefs.why: One wet autumn buys time for hydropower and Lower Basin users but does not settle the cuts that the next operating guidelines must allocate.

briefs.headline: Saudi Water Authority cancels Wabag's $272 million Yanbu desalination award for a second time
briefs.text: VA Tech Wabag disclosed on November 14 that the Saudi Water Authority cancelled its award for a 300 MLD seawater reverse osmosis plant at Yanbu, worth about $272 million, citing internal reasons on its side before countersigning. Wabag first won the plant in September 2024 at about $317 million; that tender was cancelled in December 2024 and re-awarded in July 2025. Shares fell 7.18% in the next session, and the company said it is seeking the reasons and next steps.
briefs.why: Saudi procurement is shifting, and EPC bidders face award risk until contracts are countersigned. It is a fresh test for this week's company in focus.

company.name: VA Tech Wabag
company.headline: Wabag's order book passed ₹20,000 crore, then Saudi Arabia pulled a big one
company.body: The Chennai based water treatment and desalination contractor reported first half revenue up 20% to about ₹1,887 crore and net profit up 29% to about ₹195 crore for the period to September 30, with net cash for a 15th straight quarter. Chairman and managing director Rajiv Mittal pointed to two large desalination orders, a seawater plant in Kuwait and a plant at Jamnagar in India. Management said revenue growth could reach the top of its 15% to 20% guidance. Nine days later the Saudi Water Authority cancelled the 300,000 cubic meter a day Yanbu award, and the company said it is seeking the reasons before deciding next steps.

leader.name: Yang Seung-jo
leader.role: Chief executive, Korea Water Resources Corporation (K-water)

figs.l: Daily supply planned for Honam fabs

leader.body: Yang has started his term at K-water's helm on the chip file. His first official field trip, on November 18, was to SK hynix's Yongin cluster to discuss timely supply and plans to localize ultrapure water production. On November 20 he inspected Juam and Dongbok dams, the main sources for the planned Honam semiconductor complex, where K-water plans to supply about 600,000 cubic meters a day and build 1.06 million of capacity to cover future demand and drought. Dongbok Dam is being raised 15 meters so it can send 300,000 cubic meters a day to the complex.

supplier.name: Kemira
supplier.headline: Kemira is buying its way into industrial water services while raw material costs squeeze margins
body: Kemira, the Helsinki based maker of coagulants, flocculants and other chemicals for water intensive industries, employs about 4,900 people. On October 23 it reported third quarter revenue of €709 million, up 3%, with flat organic growth and about €18 million added by acquisitions. Chief executive Antti Salminen kept full year guidance of €2.6 to €3.0 billion in revenue and €400 to €500 million in operative EBITDA.

Water Solutions, its largest segment, grew revenue 5% to €331 million, mainly through acquisitions, with a 19.7% operative EBITDA margin. Kemira closed the purchase of Nebraska based Water Engineering, an industrial water treatment services firm serving food and beverage, manufacturing and healthcare, in October 2025, then added ANMAC Water Treatment Service and Italy's REPUR, which provides activated carbon services, in the third quarter.

The pressure is on costs. Group operative EBITDA margin fell to 15.9% from 20.0% as variable costs rose €35 million against €11 million of price increases, and Kemira puts the gross 2026 cost impact of the Middle East conflict at about €100 million, roughly half of it mitigated. On November 23 it said it will invest in a venture fund to back startup innovation.
supplier.why: Activated carbon and service contracts put Kemira closer to the PFAS and industrial reuse spending wave. Watch whether price increases catch up with input costs in 2027.

innovation.name: Claros Technologies
innovation.headline: Claros takes PFAS destruction to full scale at Daikin
innovation.body: Most PFAS treatment moves the chemicals into another waste stream. Claros breaks them apart with its ClarosTechUV system. On October 1 it signed a commercial agreement with Daikin America for full-scale deployment at Daikin's plant in Decatur, Alabama, after a December 2025 run treated more than 170,000 gallons of process water with greater than 99.99% destruction of target PFAS.

investor.name: Burnt Island Ventures
investor.headline: The most active water-only venture firm
investor.body: Founded in New York by water industry veteran Tom Ferguson, Burnt Island invests only in early stage water technology. Xylem anchored both of its funds, with climate fund of funds WovenEarth Ventures joining Fund II. Published deal trackers show 2026 investments in Aquatic Labs, Crew Carbon, Biota and Verdi.

capital.intro: Private equity has executed 435 water deals across 25 countries since 2015 and more than doubled its holdings since 2019, according to Bluefield Research. Most of those assets are under three years old, which points to an exit wave.

security.headline: The UN says the world has entered water bankruptcy
security.text: A UN University report in January argued that groundwater depletion, overallocation and pollution have pushed many basins past the point of recovery, and that "crisis" no longer describes it.

security.headline: The Gulf runs on desalination
security.text: The Middle East and North Africa host over 40% of global desalination capacity, and the Gulf Cooperation Council countries alone hold 33%.

place.name: Basilica Cistern
place.headline: A sixth century reservoir held up by a forest of 336 columns
body: Built between 532 and 542 under the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian I, the Basilica Cistern, Yerebatan Sarnıcı in Turkish, was one of the city's major water stores, with an estimated capacity of about 100,000 tons. Its roof rests on 336 columns, each 9 meters tall.

Two carved Medusa heads, identified in 1986, serve as column bases, one upside down and one on its side. The cistern opened to visitors in 1987 after a major restoration, and reopened on July 22, 2022 after a second restoration that began in 2014.
place.visit: In Istanbul's historic peninsula; open as a museum. Check opening hours and tickets before you go.
place.why: Istanbul hosts the IWRA World Water Congress in October 2027, and this is the city's oldest lesson in storing water close to demand.
